title: Cardamom and farm life in South Sikkim
meta_description: Large cardamom under alder shade, smoky bhatti kilns, oranges, dalle chilli and fermented foods: the South Sikkim farm year and how to see it on a homestay.
summary: Large cardamom, grown in shady gullies under alder trees and dried over wood smoke, has been the cash crop of Sikkim's hill farms for generations; Sikkim was once the world's biggest producer. In South Sikkim's villages you can see it picked from August to November, alongside oranges, ginger, maize, dalle chillies and home-fermented foods.

sections.heading: The spice behind Sikkim's hill farms
paras: Drive any road below Ravangla or around Yangang and Borong and look into the damp, shaded gullies. Under tall trees with pale bark you will see clumps of broad leaves, waist to head high, like a small banana or ginger plant. That is large cardamom, Amomum subulatum, called alaichi in Nepali, and for much of the twentieth century it paid for school fees, roofs and weddings across rural Sikkim.

It is a different spice from the small green cardamom of South India. The pods are large, dark brown and wrinkled, and they are dried over fire, which gives them a smoky, camphor-like flavour. Most of the crop goes to the plains, where it flavours garam masala, biryani and meat curries. According to a 2016 study in the journal Mountain Research and Development, Declining Large Cardamom Production Systems in the Sikkim Himalayas, Sikkim was the world's largest producer until the early 2000s, when production began to fall.

sections.heading: How it is grown: shade, alder and smoke
paras: Large cardamom needs shade, moisture and cool air, which is why it grows in north-facing slopes, stream banks and gullies, typically between about 600 and 2,000 m. The classic shade tree is utis, the Himalayan alder (Alnus nepalensis), which fixes nitrogen in the soil and drops leaf litter that feeds the crop. Agricultural scientists often hold up the alder-cardamom system as a model of mountain farming that protects slopes and soil while earning cash. Growers in Sikkim recognise several local varieties, among them Ramsai, Golsai, Sawney and Varlangey, each suited to different heights.

Harvest runs from about August at lower farms to November higher up. Pickers cut the spikes at the base of the plant, strip the pods and carry them in baskets to the bhatti, a traditional kiln built of stone and mud, where they are dried over a slow wood fire for a day or more. The smoke is what gives Sikkim's cardamom its character, though improved kilns that dry more cleanly have been promoted in recent decades.

sections.heading: Boom, blight and what farmers face now
paras: The decline after the early 2000s had several causes that the research literature names: viral diseases known locally as chirke and foorkey, fungal leaf blight, ageing plantations, lack of fresh planting material, and changing rainfall and temperature. Down To Earth magazine reported farmers whose harvests had fallen to a third of what the same land once gave, and many families shifted part of their land to vegetables, ginger, oranges or fodder, or sent younger members to work in towns.

Prices add to the uncertainty. Large cardamom is traded in a volatile market, and the price farmers receive has swung widely from year to year, sometimes by half. A good season can still bring in more than any other crop on the same land, which is why so many households keep at least a patch. When you see pods drying in a homestay courtyard, you are looking at much of that family's cash income for the year.

sections.heading: Beyond cardamom: the rest of the farm
paras: A South Sikkim hill farm is rarely one crop. Around the house are terraces of maize, the staple of the middle hills, with finger millet and rice lower down; vegetable plots of squash (iskus), beans, mustard greens and radish; and orange trees, whose fruit ripens from November to January. Ginger and turmeric grow on the warmer slopes, and broom grass (amliso) on the steep edges, cut in winter for brooms sold in the plains. Most families keep a cow or two, goats and chickens.

Then there is dalle khursani, the small, round, fiercely hot red chilli that appears in pickles on every Sikkimese table. Sikkim has farmed without chemical fertilisers and pesticides as state policy since it was declared a fully organic state in January 2016, so most of what you eat on a village stay is grown a few steps from the kitchen.
list: Ginger: harvested late in the year, after the monsoon
Maize: planted spring, harvested late summer
Dalle khursani: picked from summer into autumn

sections.heading: The fermented kitchen
paras: Hill farms had to store food through long monsoons and cold winters, and the answer was fermentation. Gundruk is leafy greens, often mustard or radish leaves, fermented and sun-dried, then cooked into a sour soup; sinki is the same idea with radish roots. Kinema is fermented soybean with a strong smell and a sticky texture, cooked with onions, tomatoes and chilli. Chhurpi, made from buttermilk, comes soft and fresh for curries or hard and dried as a chew. These are everyday foods, not curiosities.

The food scientist Jyoti Prakash Tamang, who has studied them for decades at Sikkim University, describes them in his book Himalayan Fermented Foods: Microbiology, Nutrition, and Ethnic Values (2010), a good source if you want the detail. On a homestay, ask your host to show you the gundruk drying or the kinema in its basket; most are delighted to explain.

sections.heading: Seeing farm life on a village stay
paras: The best way to understand all this is to stay with a farming family for two nights. Kewzing, Yangang and Borong near Ravangla all have homestays where hosts are happy to walk you through their fields, explain what grows where, and in season let you watch or help with the cardamom harvest and drying. October and November are ideal: harvest time, clear skies and the start of the orange season. Expect to pay about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals.

A few courtesies help. Ask before you walk into a field or photograph people working; stay on the bunds and paths; never pick fruit or pods without asking. If you want to buy cardamom, oranges, chilli pickle or local tea, buy directly from your hosts or at the Namchi market rather than at roadside stalls aimed at tourists, so the money goes to the people who grew it. Prices vary with the season.

sections.heading: Taking the flavours home
paras: Large cardamom keeps well in an airtight jar for a year or more; crush a pod into rice, dal or a meat curry. Dalle khursani pickle travels well in a sealed jar, though airlines may ask you to pack it in checked baggage. Dried gundruk is light and easy to carry; soak it and cook it with potato, tomato and garlic for a sour soup. Temi tea, from Sikkim's own estate a short drive away, completes the set. All of these are sold in Namchi and Gangtok, and many homestays sell their own.

faqs.q: What is large cardamom and how is it different from green cardamom?
faqs.a: Large cardamom (Amomum subulatum) is a different plant from the small green cardamom of South India. Its pods are big, dark brown and wrinkled, and in Sikkim they are dried over wood smoke, giving a smoky, camphor-like flavour used in garam masala, biryani and meat curries. Sikkim was once its largest producer.

faqs.q: When is the cardamom harvest in Sikkim?
faqs.a: From about August at lower-altitude farms to November higher up, with October the peak in most South Sikkim villages. Pods are dried in traditional bhatti kilns over wood smoke on the day of harvest. A homestay stay in October or November is the best time to see it.

faqs.q: Why has cardamom production in Sikkim declined?
faqs.a: Researchers cite viral diseases known as chirke and foorkey, fungal leaf blight, ageing plantations, shortage of healthy planting material and changing rainfall. Since the early 2000s many families have moved part of their land to vegetables, ginger and oranges. Volatile prices add to the pressure.

faqs.q: Why is cardamom grown under alder trees?
faqs.a: Large cardamom needs shade and moisture. The Himalayan alder, called utis, gives light shade, fixes nitrogen in the soil and drops nutritious leaf litter, so the two grow well together. The system also holds steep slopes and soil in place, which is why scientists value it.

faqs.q: Can I visit a cardamom farm in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes, the easiest way is a homestay in a farming village such as Kewzing, Yangang or Borong near Ravangla. Hosts usually walk guests through their fields and, from August to November, let them watch the harvest and drying. Expect about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals.

Gundruk is leafy greens, usually mustard or radish leaves, fermented for several days and then sun-dried. It is cooked into a sour soup or pickle and is an everyday food across Sikkim and the Nepali-speaking Himalaya. Food scientist Jyoti Prakash Tamang has written about it in detail.

Sikkim was declared a fully organic state in January 2016, and chemical fertilisers and pesticides are restricted by state policy. On village farms most vegetables, grains and spices are grown with manure and compost. In towns, some produce is brought from outside the state.

Dalle khursani is a small, round, very hot red chilli grown across Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills. It is eaten fresh, dried and above all in pickles, and you will find a jar on almost every Sikkimese table. Ask for food without it if you prefer mild cooking.

faqs.q: Where can I buy cardamom and local produce in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: At the Namchi market, from your homestay hosts, or at government and cooperative outlets in Namchi and Gangtok. Buying directly from farming families or the main markets means the money reaches the growers. Prices vary by season and quality.
